01.note: Rafram, who lived in Pumbedita, gave his firstborn animal to a priest while it was still unblemished, and the priest went and caused a blemish in it himself. Later the priest brought that same animal to Rafram, as an expert, to have it declared fit to slaughter, claiming an Israelite had given it to him already blemished. Rafram's eyes were afflicted that day, but he forced them open, recognized the animal, and said: Is it not I who gave this to you? Even so, the Gemara says, Rafram was unconcerned: only this priest was impudent, and other priests are not.
01.why: The Gemara has just ruled that a priest is believed when he says an Israelite gave him a firstborn already blemished. Rafram's case shows one priest lying, yet Rafram still did not doubt other priests, so the ruling stands.

people.name: Rafram
people.about: A man in Pumbedita who gave his firstborn animal to a priest and later served as the expert examining it.

people.name: the priest
people.about: Received Rafram's firstborn, blemished it himself, then claimed an Israelite had given it to him that way.

terms.meaning: The first male calf, lamb or kid born to an animal belongs to a priest and is sacred. It may be slaughtered and eaten as ordinary meat only if it has a permanent blemish, and deliberately causing a blemish is forbidden.
A physical defect that disqualifies an animal from being offered on the altar. An expert had to examine and confirm it before the animal could be eaten.

02.note: Rabbi Yosei recalled an incident in Piran of Beit Menahem. A firstborn animal seemed to have only one testicle; someone pressed its sac and the second testicle did not come out. When the animal was slaughtered, the testicle was found attached to the loins. Rabbi Akiva permitted the meat and Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri forbade it. Rabbi Akiva said to him: Until when will you waste the property of the Jewish people? Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri answered: Until when will you feed the Jewish people carcasses?
02.why: The mishna mentions this incident briefly after Rabbi Akiva's test of pressing the sac; the Gemara brings a fuller account from a baraita, then asks how Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri could call properly slaughtered animals carcasses.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident in the baraita.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Permitted the animal's meat and accused his colleague of wasting people's property.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri
people.about: Forbade the meat and accused Rabbi Akiva of feeding people carcasses.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core legal collection, and is quoted in the Gemara as an authority.
The first male born to a cow, sheep or goat is sacred and goes to a priest. It may be slaughtered and eaten outside the Temple only if it has a blemish, such as a missing testicle.
Meat of an animal that died without proper ritual slaughter, which is forbidden to eat.

03.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi once decided a real case following the view of Rabbi Eliezer: a woman who has gone three expected cycles without bleeding is not made impure retroactively when she bleeds again. Afterward he remembered that other Sages disagreed with Rabbi Eliezer, and he said: Rabbi Eliezer is worthy to rely upon in exigent circumstances. The Gemara then asks what it was that he remembered.
03.why: The Gemara is testing Rav Huna's view that a menstruating woman's retroactive impurity does not affect teruma. This case, which must have involved teruma, implies the majority view makes teruma impure retroactively, contradicting Rav Huna.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; ruled in this case according to Rabbi Eliezer and then reconsidered.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage whose lenient view Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi followed; other Sages disagreed with him.

terms.meaning: A situation of pressing need, when a minority opinion may be relied on even though the law normally follows the majority.
The rule that a woman who finds menstrual blood may be treated as having been ritually impure for a period before she noticed it, affecting pure foods she touched in that time.

03.flag: The last story segment continues into the Gemara's analysis of the case ("And we discussed it..."), which runs on past the end of the story.

04.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi examined a woman's blood at night and declared it impure. Looking at it again by day, he declared it pure. He waited an hour and declared it impure again. Then he said: Woe is me! Perhaps I erred.
04.why: The Gemara is discussing how Sages examined blood and whether one may rule on it based on how it would have looked earlier; it questions his worry, citing a rule that one may not say the blood would have been impure had it been moist, and then rereads the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; examined the blood three times, changed his ruling twice and feared he had erred.

terms.meaning: A woman who found a stain could bring it to a Sage, who judged by its color whether it was menstrual blood making her ritually impure, or a color that leaves her pure.
Ritual status, not hygiene. A woman who is impure from menstruation may not have relations with her husband or touch certain sacred foods until she purifies herself.
